elements.text: Here cold is produced by heat, like in a gas refrigerator. The chamber does not dump heat, it consumes it: heat is its fuel. A 5×5×5 multiblock: casing floor and ceiling, cryo panels for walls, a column of refrigeration chambers inside and the core at the front.

The core sits in the front row of the floor and sets the orientation of the whole build — the chamber assembles the same way in any direction. ANY casing block accepts heat, so pipes can be routed into the floor and ceiling at several points at once.

The chamber is an installation, not a machine: it accumulates DEPTH. Depth follows the heat inflow and settles exactly on it, so the stages read directly in heat per tick: 200, 800 and 1800. It builds over minutes of steady supply and drops three times faster, so the chamber is never switched off.

The module in the core sets the ceiling: without one the chamber will not go past stage one, however much heat you feed it. Module III is built from Module II and a cryo crystal, and the crystal is a stage-two product. Only those who worked a stage below are let deeper.

Three rods in the core speed the work up, from a quarter to double. They wear out, and the deeper the chamber sits the faster: nine times faster on stage three than on stage one. Depth costs more than heat alone.
The only machine that goes from fluid to item. Coolant with aluminum dust yields cryolite, the base of the whole branch: panels, casing, rods and modules all come from it.

The chamber needs coolant: it passes through and comes out hot. Pump the spent coolant out, a full tank halts the work. It is not waste but a component of late builds, starting with the Cryogenic Heat Exchanger.
